extracted.intended_audience: students and teachers of moral philosophy; readers interested in ethical theory and moral education
extracted.subtask_short: evaluating moral worth and moral education
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts criteria and methodological rules for judging the moral worth of actions and for cultivating moral disposition (methodology of pure practical reason) as presented by Kant. Includes guidance for moral pedagogy, assessment of motives, and the methodological program for a science of practical wisdom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral worth lies in acting from duty (purity of motive)
rubrics_metrics.description: An action has moral worth only if its maxim is the law itself — done from respect for the moral law (duty) rather than from inclination, self-interest, or hope of happiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant repeatedly insists that legality of action can arise without morality of character; moral worth springs from the direct conception of the law and the objective necessity of obeying it as duty. Examples: heroic conduct admired only when motive is pure; any admixture of motives taken from our own happiness hinders the influence of the moral law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present the law in purity to make it subjectively practical
rubrics_metrics.description: To make the laws of pure practical reason influence the will, they must be presented to minds unmixed with appeals to advantage, pleasure, or fear — the pure moral motive must be brought before the mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Roundabout or indirect recommendations (appealing to self-interest or threats) may produce legal compliance but not moral character. Preparatory guidance (appeals to advantage/fear) may be necessary for degraded minds, but must be followed by introduction of pure moral motive to cultivate genuine moral disposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish objective conformity from subjective moral worth
rubrics_metrics.description: When judging actions, one must ask (a) whether the action objectively conforms to the moral law and to which law, and (b) whether it was subjectively done for the sake of the moral law (i.e., whether the maxim confers moral worth).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This twofold judgement trains practical reason: first evaluate conformity (identifying the law), then examine the maxim/motive. Both aspects are necessary: correctness as deed and moral worth as disposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate kinds of duties and laws (leges obligandi vs leges obligantibus)
rubrics_metrics.description: One should distinguish laws that merely furnish a principle of obligation from those that are really obligatory — for example, duties arising from people's wants versus duties arising from their rights (essential vs non-essential duties).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This analytic distinction helps determine which obligations are essential and which are optional/non-essential when multiple duties meet in the same action; critical for correct moral judgement and pedagogy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use habitual moral judgement as pedagogical method
rubrics_metrics.description: Make judging actions by moral laws a natural, habitual employment accompanying free actions and the observation of others, sharpening judgement through practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises should ask whether actions conform to the law and whether their maxims are from duty. Habitual practice produces interest in the law of reason and helps form moral dispositions by familiarizing students with moral judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach by critical examination of biographies and examples (comparison with law)
rubrics_metrics.description: Educators should compile biographies and instances of duties and use comparison of similar actions under different circumstances to exercise pupils' critical judgement about moral significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer comparing actions to the moral law rather than relying on exemplars of 'noble' deeds. Early youth can be engaged with such critical exercises, leading to esteem for purity of motive and disgust for deviation. Avoid presenting super-meritorious examples that distract from duty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid over-emphasis on super-meritorious (noble) actions in education
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not make examples revolve around so-called noble or super-meritorious actions which inspire romantic longing for inaccessible perfection; instead, refer all to duty and everyday obligations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presenting only heroic deeds risks producing 'fantastical romancers' and causes common duties to seem petty, undermining steady moral development. Instead emphasize subjection of heart to duty and the worth consciousness gives a person.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative perfection: purity of will as absence of inclination's influence
rubrics_metrics.description: One aspect of moral character to cultivate is negative perfection — ensuring that, in actions done from duty, motives of inclination exert no determining influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises should focus attention on renouncing inclinations and experiencing the consciousness of freedom and independence from inclinations; this cultivates self-respect and a stable foundation for other moral dispositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Receptivity for pure moral interest exists and must be cultivated
rubrics_metrics.description: Human minds are capable of a receptivity for a pure moral interest; when properly applied, the pure conception of virtue is the most powerful spring for moral conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although initial attraction to duty may be weak, repeated exposure and proper method (habituation, examples of pure moral resolutions) can engender a purely moral interest that becomes the primary motivator of conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral admiration depends on cost and purity, not on pretended inward greatness
rubrics_metrics.description: Admiration and esteem for moral exemplars rest on the purity of the moral principle and the sacrifice it costs, not on displays of inward greatness or sentimental magnanimity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The effect on spectators is strongest when motives are unmixed with self-interested merit; duty — not claimed merit — produces the most penetrating influence on observers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not presuppose inclination; moral law demands obedience from duty
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral law requires obedience from duty, not from predilection or presumed inclinations; one should not assume that inclination already aligns with duty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because obedience often requires self-denial and continuous vigilance against relapse, moral education must emphasize duty itself rather than comfort, feeling, or inclination as the basis for action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate self-respect via consciousness of freedom (guard against self-contempt)
rubrics_metrics.description: By making moral judgement habitual and cultivating obedience from duty, individuals develop a consciousness of freedom and self-respect; fearing self-contempt on self-examination becomes a guard for moral dispositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a person dreads being worthless in their own eyes, other moral dispositions can be grafted on this foundation. Training should aim to make this self-assessment salient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological program for a science of practical wisdom
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop a critical, methodical science of morality: analyze moral judgements into elementary conceptions, separate empirical from rational elements, and use repeated 'experiments on common sense' (analogous to chemistry) to determine what each element can accomplish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant advises adopting a methodical, critical approach (not speculative or visionary) akin to mathematics/chemistry to prevent fanaticism and produce a reliable doctrine of practical wisdom appropriate for teachers and public understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: First engage cognitive interest, then cultivate interest in morality itself
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin moral training by engaging the faculty of judgement (pleasure in exercising cognitive powers and discerning harmony), which gives virtue a form of beauty; subsequently use living exhibition of moral character to convert that cognitive interest into an interest in morality itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Initial exercises may produce admiration without genuine moral pursuit (laudatur et alget); educators must follow up cognition-based appreciation with examples stressing purity of will so that admiration becomes motivation.
